name: Bias in Clinical Triage
title: Bias in Clinical Triage
answer: Bias in clinical triage covers the ways an automated system that sorts, scores or prioritises patients can produce systematically different outcomes for different groups. It sits inside the wider governance of medical AI, alongside device regulation, post market surveillance and clinical validation. The concern is not only the model itself but the data it learned from, the workflow it is dropped into and the staff who act on its output. Triage is a high stakes setting because a wrong ranking can delay care for the patients who need it most.

sections.body: Bias in clinical triage covers the ways an automated system that sorts, scores or prioritises patients can produce systematically different outcomes for different groups. It sits inside the wider governance of medical AI, alongside device regulation, post market surveillance and clinical validation. The concern is not only the model itself but the data it learned from, the workflow it is dropped into and the staff who act on its output. Triage is a high stakes setting because a wrong ranking can delay care for the patients who need it most.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems usually run as software modules inside an electronic health record, a triage dashboard or a hospital command centre, drawing on vitals, laboratory results, nursing notes and prior encounters. Some are deployed as standalone tools cleared or approved as medical devices, others as clinical decision support embedded in a vendor platform. Performance depends on the completeness and consistency of the input data, which varies by site, by department and by how busy the shift is. The site tracks 1,000 medical AI models, a reminder of how many of these tools now sit in or near clinical workflows.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Bias is measured by comparing model performance across subgroups defined by age, sex, race, ethnicity, language, insurance status and disability, using metrics such as sensitivity, calibration and time to treatment. Teams audit training data for historical inequities, test for proxy variables that stand in for protected characteristics, and run subgroup analyses before and after deployment. Because triage labels are often themselves the product of past clinical decisions, the reference standard can carry the same bias the model is meant to avoid. Ongoing monitoring, not a one time validation, is the usual way this is handled in practice.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: In the United States, triage software can fall under FDA device oversight, while in the European Union it falls under the Medical Device Regulation and, where patient data is processed, the GDPR.Documentation of training data, known limitations and subgroup performance is expected in submissions and in procurement. The site also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how quickly a clinical harm can move from a governance question into litigation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work is moving toward continuous bias monitoring, standardised reporting of subgroup performance and clearer expectations for post market surveillance of triage tools. Regulators and health systems are pushing for transparency about training populations and for human review of high stakes rankings. Better data collection on race, ethnicity, language and social factors is a prerequisite for measuring fairness, and many institutions are still catching up. The direction is toward triage systems that are audited as routinely as they are updated, with accountability shared between the vendor, the clinician and the institution.
